the dominant force in image classification, yet their massive parameter counts and computational demands create significant deployment hurdles, particularly on resource-constrained devices. To address this, researchers have turned to post-training pruning methods that trim superfluous parameters while keeping the model's performance largely intact. We introduce ConvPruner, an innovative approach designed specifically for image classification. Unlike previous methods, ConvPruner uniquely handles the pruning of both filters and channels within each convolutional layer. It accomplishes this in two distinct stages: first, it eliminates redundant filters guided by connection sparsity patterns; second, it removes unimportant channels based on the pruning-induced weight distributions. Our analysis reveals that the resulting sparse filters offer more granular performance control and higher expressiveness compared to standard channels. Extensive experiments across various CNN architectures and pruning strategies validate the effectiveness of ConvPruner. Notably, when applied to the ResNet50 architecture, ConvPruner removed 69.04 million parameters—achieving a 51.33% compression ratio—and successfully reduced computational complexity by 43.13%, all without compromising overall model accuracy significantly.

To address this limitation and affordably expand the computational realm, we propose utilizing the more practical and economical 3D-Cavity Quantum Electrodynamics (QED) system. By integrating a Transmon qubit within a 3D cavity and positioning it near a perfectly conducting planar interface that supports various micro- and nanostructures, we demonstrate a feasible path to achieving all necessary single- and two-qubit logic gates within 3D-Cavity QED. Crucially, the positioning of the transmon allows for the independent and tunable control of coupling strengths between the qubits and specific cavity modes as well as direct inter-qubit interactions. We further show that utilizing only two transmon qubits is sufficient to operate an effective dipolar two-level dipole (D2) artificial atom situated on the conductor plane, thereby emulating a true two-wavelength superconducting artifact within this compact architecture. A prominent advantage of this hybrid setup is its simplicity of design compared to current multi-cavity schemes. We provide a detailed analysis of the required geometrical parameters to validate the feasibility of our configuration and confirm that proposed parameters can execute a full quantum computation cycle in under 1 microsecond while simultaneously preserving a joint quantum lifetime exceeding 1 hour.

A widely adopted model for these processes is the Cox process conditioned on a latent intensity that follows a Dynamic Linear Model (DLM). While these processes can also be described using the Markov Switching Autoregressive (MS-ARD) process—where the intensity depends on a hidden Markov state with transition probabilities determined by a Gibbs kernel—a key limitation of the MS-ARD model is its computational intractability for large event types due to a state space partitioning algorithm that scales exponentially with the number of activity states, a drawback that limits applications like high-cardinality neural coding studies. In this paper, we introduce an exact and efficient process that conditions on a latent intensity driven by a DLM to generate timed events. This process offers a flexible framework for data analysis that is both computationally efficient and data-adaptive, making it especially appropriate for handling large-scale datasets.

graph neural networks (GNNs) theoretically rely on a fixed grid-like architecture, which has led to widespread speculation that their success stems merely by implicitly matching a optimal grid-based inductive bias. This study offers a rigorous exploration into how the implicit induction bias functions within GNNs. We demonstrate that these models do not simply treat data as grid-based; rather, they effectively conceptually map irregular data onto implicit graph structures. We establish a formal connection between the smoothing characteristics typical of GNNs and the properties of the classical heat equation in continuous spatial and temporal domains. Furthermore, we introduce a novel class of network designs dedicated to simulating the heat equation precisely, verifying that these new additions significantly surpass current state-of-the-art methods across various tasks involving geometric data.
